analysis.title: US Watch: Sep jobs: Wake me up when seasonals end
key_insights: Sep NFP was +29k with the unemployment rate at 4.2%. BofA calls the report soft but not surprising given the weak seasonals it had anticipated.
Private payrolls rose 46k, close to BofA's below-consensus forecast of 50k. After downward revisions, the three-month average job gain is 50k, still above breakeven.

The Sep seasonal adjustment was more punitive than in 2025 and 2024. It subtracted 304k jobs versus 229k a year earlier, likely payback for Aug's unusually favorable seasonal factor. NSA job growth was stronger than in Sep 2025.
One explanation for the seasonal swing is the survey calendar. Aug 2026 fell in a four-week survey interval year versus five weeks in 2024 and 2025. BofA says underlying job growth remains steady.
Leisure and hospitality added 10k (Aug: 37k) and local government education fell 2k (Aug: +49k, likely school calendar changes). These two categories drove most of the Aug upside surprise.

Education and health added 20k and has slowed recently. Goods-producing jobs grew steadily, led by construction (+11k) and manufacturing (+9k), which BofA ties to data center investment and defense spending. Trade, transport and utilities added 18k, likely on higher imports.

The unrounded unemployment rate rose only from 4.14% to 4.17%. Household employment rose 406k (Aug: 569k) and the labor force participation rate rose two-tenths to 61.8%. U2 and U6 slack measures fell.

Average hourly earnings slowed to 0.1% m/m from 0.3% with average weekly hours unchanged. The index of aggregate weekly payrolls slowed a tenth to 4.2% y/y. BofA calls wages the most dovish part of the report.

The report was not soft enough to shift the Fed's focus from inflation. BofA says risks have shifted away from its call for an October hike and it will revisit the call after the Sep inflation releases.

Rates: the curve bull steepened, with 2Y and 10Y yields down 6-7bps and the 30Y down 4bps. Most of the move came from lower real rates. BofA says the data challenges its pay-2Y view and curve flattening bias.

FX: the dollar softened only about 0.2% against most G10 currencies. DXY was up about 2.5% in September and recently hit its highest level since May 2025. BofA says Sep CPI (due 14 Oct) will matter more for the dollar than this report.
